Max Kettner, among Wall Street’s most bullish strategists, is cutting back on his bet on stocks for the first time in months, arguing that sharp mood changes among investors warrant a more cautious approach ahead of next week’s US midterms.
The HSBC Holdings Plc chief multi-asset strategist, who has described his stance in previous client notes as “Max Bullish,” on Monday tactically reduced his stock allocation to neutral from maximum overweight for the first time since mid-March.

Stocks started the week on a positive note as crude oil retreated from a six-month high and investors awaited a busy slate of tech earnings for a steer on the artificial intelligence trade.
Futures on the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100 edged higher following two weeks of steep tech losses, which saw a US gauge of semiconductor stocks sink to a three-month low. Meta Platforms Inc. shares climbed in premarket trading after the company said it plans to raise as much as $95 billion for AI development through stock sales, with Nvidia Corp., Broadcom Inc. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. among prospective buyers.

Indian refiners are increasingly turning to Persian Gulf crude and pulling back from their mainstay supplier Russia, as sky-high freight costs erode the economics of long-haul shipments.
Some Iraqi cargoes are being sold at discounts of more than $25 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark before shipping, according to traders involved in the talks. On a delivered basis, that translates into discounts of several dollars a barrel to Dated Brent. Russian crude, by comparison, is being offered at about a $2 premium to the benchmark, making purchases from India’s biggest supplier uneconomical, the traders said, asking not to be named discussing commercially sensitive information.

Soybean futures fell to a two-month low in Chicago, while coffee and sugar slumped as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise election win in Brazil hit the nation’s currency, boosting export prospects for the commodity powerhouse.
Lula won a fourth term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a political upset that comes as a setback to investors who had backed his rival to rein in the country’s deficit. Brazilian markets are heading for a rout when local trading begins with a currency derivatives contract on the CME exchange showing the real at 5.60 a dollar, which implies a 12% plunge from Friday’s close. Trading on the real opens at 8 a.m. New York time.

Borr Drilling Ltd. shares fell 11% after one of its rigs sank off the African nation of Gabon over the weekend.
The Prospector 5 jackup rig had an incident the night of Oct. 24 when it was preparing for drilling operations, Borr said in a statement on Sunday. The crew of 115 experienced a “punch through event” that resulted in a loss of stability and subsequent sinking, it said, citing preliminary information.

Brazil’s surprise election result dominated emerging markets as the nation’s dollar bonds tumbled in London. Developing-nation stocks and currencies elsewhere were little changed.
Several Brazilian dollar bonds were among the worst performers in emerging markets, with the yield on notes due in 2037 jumping 19 basis points to 6.44%. Investors are bracing for a broader repricing when local markets open after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva unexpectedly won a fourth presidential term, defying expectations for a Bolsonaro victory that had fueled a rally in Brazilian assets earlier this month.
